item.title: Imaginary quadratic fields of class number at most 2000
item.dc:creator: Iwao Kimura
item.description:
Proves an explicit Landau–Siegel zero gap and an imaginary quadratic class-number lower bound in Lean 4 with Mathlib, checked by the Lean kernel and the independent nanoda kernel.
We determine all imaginary quadratic fields with class number at most 2000, unconditionally: there are 16,453,493 of them, and the largest $|d_K|$ among them is 1,062,350,083. To our knowledge, such a list was previously known only for class number at most 100. We make explicit a recent argument, released by OpenAI and not refereed, that excludes Landau-Siegel zeros: every real zero $β$ of $L(s,χ)$, for a primitive real character $χ$ of conductor $q\ge3$, satisfies $(1-β)\log q\ge5.8\cdot10^{-4}$. An elementary lower bound for $L(1,χ)$ then shows that a field with class number at most 2000 has $|d_K|<1.61\cdot10^{15}$. The fields with $6\cdot2^{28}\le|d_K|\le1.65\cdot10^{15}$ are excluded by Watkins' sieve, and those below are read from the class group tables of Mosunov and Jacobson. As a consequence, the lists of Cremona and Sutherland of imaginary quadratic orders with class number at most 1000, and the counts of Holmin, Jones, Kurlberg, McLeman and Petersen for odd class numbers up to 1999, previously known under the generalized Riemann hypothesis, hold unconditionally. The two steps, the bound for $β$ and the bound for $|d_K|$, are proved in Lean, building on the existing formalization of that argument, and the proofs are checked by two independent kernels. The contributions of AI systems to this work are stated in the paper.

item.title: Poisson statistics for one-dimensional Anderson–Bernoulli Schrödinger operators
item.dc:creator: Yi Han
item.description:
The main Poisson statistics theorem has an end-to-end Lean 4 formalization using Mathlib, checked by Lean's kernel and released as a public repository.
We prove Poisson local eigenvalue statistics for one-dimensional Schrödinger operators with nondegenerate Bernoulli potentials at any fixed nonzero coupling. After unfolding by the integrated density of states (IDS), the local eigenvalue process converges to a Poisson point process of unit intensity at every energy in the interior of the almost-sure spectrum. The theorem also holds for bounded nonconstant iid potentials, provided the IDS is continuous and strictly increasing near the reference energy. If the IDS also has a finite positive derivative at that energy, the usual linear normalization gives the same limit. The proof uses a phase coordinate with exact IDS drift to obtain a uniform exponential crossing law and joint Poisson counts in disjoint energy windows.

item.title: Explicit reduced APN permutations: ramification and optimal Galois-ring lifts
item.dc:creator: Hiroki Fukui
item.description:
Key statements about the APN permutation family are formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib, sorry-free, with sources and blueprint deposited on Zenodo.
Let $m\ge5$ be odd and $q=2^m$. For every odd $r$ with $3\le r<m$ and $\gcd(r,m)=1$ we give the reduced polynomial $P_{m,r}=\mathrm{red}((T_r^3)^{2^{m-2}})$, $T_r=\sum_{i<r}X^{2^i}$, explicitly: it has coefficients in $\mathbb{F}_2$ and exactly $3r-2$ terms, it is an APN permutation of $\mathbb{F}_q$, and its formal derivative $1+X^{2^{r-2}}+X^{2^{m-2}}$ has no zero on $\mathbb{F}_q$ and is two-to-one. We determine the ramification of $P_{m,r}$ as a map of the projective line for all admissible $(m,r)$: there are $2^{m-r}$ finite ramification points, all wild, with index and different exponent $2^{r-2}$, all over the single finite branch value $1$. The $0/1$ lift of $P_{m,r}$ satisfies an identity in $\mathbb{Z}[X]$ that evaluates it over every Galois ring $\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)$ with $m-1$ squarings, one general multiplication and $r+5$ additions or subtractions. For every quadratic optimal APN permutation $p$ of $\mathbb{F}_q$ (in particular $P_{m,r}$), every $k\ge2$ and every coefficient lift $F$ of $p$ to $\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)$, we determine the differential rows of $F$ exactly in the unit directions whose residue lies outside the kernel $\{0,ρ\}$ of the linear part of $p'$ (they are the residue rows of $p$; $ρ=1$ for $P_{m,r}$) and in the directions in $2^{k-1}\mathrm{GR}(2^k,m)\setminus\{0\}$ (every nonzero entry equals $2q^{k-1}$). We also give a self-contained proof of the Li–Wang criterion for a Gold function plus a linearised polynomial, which explains why the inner map of $P_{m,r}$ is not a monomial, and record a two-word, two-layer transition that a simple linear layer forbids at the residue level.

item.title: Optimal Reduced Representatives of Quadratic APN Permutations in Odd Dimension
item.dc:creator: Hiroki Fukui
item.description:
The Main Theorem for odd n≥9 is formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using Mathlib's Schwartz–Zippel bound, and checked with lean4checker.
The formal derivative of the reduced polynomial representative of a map on a binary finite field depends on the coordinates, although its differential uniformity does not. This matters for lifting permutations to Galois rings: a polynomial over a Galois ring of characteristic a power of two greater than two permutes the ring exactly when its reduction permutes the residue field and the derivative of the reduction has no zero there. We prove that for every odd $n\ge5$, every quadratic almost perfect nonlinear permutation $Q$ of $\mathbb{F}_{2^n}$ admits invertible binary-linear maps $L$ and $A$ such that the derivative of the reduced representative of $L\circ Q\circ A$ has no zero and each of its nonempty fibres has exactly two elements. The range is exact: this fails for $n=3$, as computed earlier, and for even $n$ there are no such permutations. For $n\ge9$, a linearization and a projectively injective cofactor map reduce the problem to counting binary matrices: more than 5% of the invertible inputs $A$ succeed, more than half for $n\ge15$, without any classification. For $n=5,7$ we use two independent classifications and finite certificates. Consequently every such permutation is linearly equivalent to a counterexample to the reduced critical-point conjecture of Bartoli and Stănică that lifts to permutation polynomials of optimal differential uniformity over every Galois ring with this residue field. For odd $n\ge9$ the existence proof is checked in the Lean 4 proof assistant.

item.title: Equality of the Jellium and the Uniform Electron Gas Energies
item.dc:creator: Mihály A. Csirik
item.description:
The lower and upper comparison proofs and the neutralization construction are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, produced with AI assistance and released in a public repository.
Jellium, a system of electrons in a uniform neutralizing background, and the uniform electron gas (UEG), a system of electrons with constant density and no background, are two standard models of the electron gas. We prove that the ground-state energy per unit volume of Jellium, as defined by Lieb and Narnhofer, coincides with the UEG energy defined by Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer, i.e. \[ e^\hbar_{\rm Jel}(ρ_0)=e^\hbar_{\rm UEG}(ρ_0). \] This equality was previously established in the classical case by Lewin, Lieb and Seiringer and independently by Cotar and Petrache.

item.title: IneqAgent: Agentic Inequality Proving in Lean with Symbolic Computation
item.dc:creator: Gaolei He, Jinhui Li, Ruobing Zuo, Xia Zeng, Zhengfeng Yang
item.description:
Builds an LLM agent that generates Lean 4 inequality proofs from symbolic certificates, with every proof checked by the Lean kernel against the original theorem statements.
Formal inequality proving requires mathematical reasoning and exact computation, often connected through intermediate lemmas and goal reformulations. We introduce IneqAgent, an agentic framework combining LLM reasoning with symbolic computation for inequality proving in Lean4. Lemma-level Monte Carlo Tree Search coordinates lemma construction, goal reformulation, and symbolic backend selection. Complementary sum-of-squares, Bernstein, and successive difference-substitution backends produce exact certificates for local Lean proof generation. The agent integrates these proofs with LLM-generated steps and uses Lean feedback to construct complete proofs checked against the original theorem statements. On four benchmarks, IneqAgent with DeepSeek-V4-Flash solves 175 of 186 problems (94.09%), achieving the highest overall success rate among the evaluated methods. Across four backbones, it achieves higher success rates at low LLM inference cost thresholds than Direct Agent using the same backbone, with lower mean inference costs over each method's successful runs. We also obtain Lean-verified strengthenings of Dittert's conjecture in dimensions four and five, and certify the Holens–Djokovic $(4,4)$ inequality, implying Merris's conjecture in dimension four.

item.title: When Correctness Feedback Erases Evidence: Phase-Separated Completeness Auditing in Verus
item.dc:creator: Adarsh Agrawal
item.description:
Lean is a secondary evaluation setting: discovery policies are run on 24 Verina Lean tasks, where the Verus no-feedback advantage does not reproduce.
Correctness feedback suppresses the very evidence that specification-completeness auditing is designed to uncover: programs that satisfy a written contract but violate intended behavior. We demonstrate this objective reversal on 12 Verus/Rust tasks across four model families under matched call budgets. Independent no-feedback discovery more than doubles certified-witness yield relative to IntentShield's corrective-feedback loop (59.0% versus 27.1%). A format-matched iterative control places the larger share of this gap in feedback content, not independent restarts. The advantage holds in every model family and survives parser repair. A separate phase-separated execution matches the aggregate yield without reusing responses; most certified witnesses also fail held-out cases. Preserving these witnesses delivers stronger specification repair: Phase-Revised contracts achieve 81.3% implementation success, versus 62.5% for IS-Revised, with Direct-Revised close behind. Both no-feedback witness sources substantially outperform weakened contracts. The effect does not reproduce in the available Dafny and Lean evaluations, establishing an empirical boundary around the studied Verus/Rust workflow. Completeness auditing and correctness repair have opposing immediate objectives. Preserve and certify the admitted failure before repairing it.

item.title: KL Before and After Mixing: A Round-Complexity Separation in Parallel Sampling
item.dc:creator: Tianyi Wu
item.description:
A Lean 4/Mathlib package (369 modules) kernel-checks the paper's key bounds, numerical brackets, and finite exhibits on parallel-sampling round complexity.
A parallel sampler can choose at random which coordinates to generate together. For a target $p$ and the output law $q_U$ of a schedule $U$ drawn afresh for each output, we compare the schedule-averaged divergence $\mathbb{E}_U D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q_U)$ with the output-law divergence $D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|\mathbb{E}_U q_U)$, in nats. Rounds commit independent draws from exact conditional marginals frozen at the round's start, each output's schedule is drawn before sampling from a finite mixture of schedules, and every scheduled round is charged. For the uniform distribution on binary strings of even length $n$ with $n/2$ ones, the least expected number of rounds at a fixed tolerance $\varepsilon>0$ is $Θ_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ under the first criterion but $(e^{-\varepsilon}+o(1))\log_2\ln n$ under the second, and the double-logarithmic order is attainable with the same round count on every run. For this target, a count-state recursion gives the exact least output divergence at every round cap over all causal randomized policies. The separation extends to weighted fixed-count targets with bounded weight ratios and quota fractions bounded away from zero and one, without permutation symmetry, and to the full-support Beta$(1,1)$–Bernoulli target, where the sharp expected cost under the output-law criterion is $(e^{-\varepsilon}/2+o(1))\log_2\log_2n$, attained with rare $n$-round runs. Prior work implies the order of the schedule-averaged cost on the balanced target and its $O_\varepsilon((\log n)^2)$ upper bounds on both extensions.

item.title: Quantitative Eshelby stability: local and finite-shape theory through AI-assisted mechanics
item.dc:creator: Bo Ni
item.description:
Selected mathematical components of the local Eshelby stability theorem are partially formalized and checked in Lean 4; the full theorem is not formally verified.
How can human researchers use artificial intelligence (AI) to make progress on difficult mechanics problems while retaining control of physical significance, mathematical rigor, and validation? We explore this opportunity through a quantitative stability problem rooted in the Eshelby conjecture. For a uniform dilatational eigenstrain in a homogeneous isotropic solid, we establish a nonlinear two-sided relation between whole-interior strain heterogeneity and a geometry-only distance from the ellipsoid family, with half-order Sobolev scaling that captures morphological length scale. We then develop a complementary finite-shape theory: ellipsoidal subtraction yields an exact residual-field budget from which systematically convergent upper and lower bounds are obtained for a prescribed geometry. Applied to protruded, indented, and necked inclusions, the bounds agree with independent displacement-based finite-element calculations. The study also documents a human-led, AI-assisted research process in which researchers select consequential problems, shape targets, audit arguments, require independent checks, and interpret mechanics, while AI broadens analytical exploration and supports computation. This experience also led us to develop Open Problems in Mechanics, a versioned community-facing map that makes selected mechanics questions, their known/open boundaries, and criteria for progress explicit.

item.title: Anechoic: Onsager-Corrected Parallel Annealing for Sub-0.1 ms Dense Max-Cut on an FPGA
item.dc:creator: Seungki Hong, Kyeongwon Jeong, Taekwang Jang
item.description:
Finite identities behind the annealing correction and the hardware engine (field updates, address mapping, cut formula) are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, and also in Rocq.
Ising machines solve combinatorial optimization problems by annealing a network of spins. On dense problems, the least expensive hardware step updates all spins at once: stochastic cellular automata (SCA) decide every spin in parallel and read couplings only for the spins that flip. Such synchronous updates create an echo: the previous state of each spin returns to it through its neighbors. On K2000, a Max-Cut benchmark on a 2,000-node complete graph, two-thirds of all flips undo the same spin's flip one step earlier. This paper presents Anechoic, an FPGA Ising machine that subtracts this echo from every decision. Dynamical mean-field theory identifies the echo as an Onsager reaction; its one-step strength is the number of spins whose flip probability is strictly between 0 and 1, divided by twice the temperature. The decision logic already flags these spins, so the correction costs one population count per step; a temperature-scaled form needs none. An RTL engine executes a dense 2,000-spin step in 18.1 cycles plus 0.14 per flip, so every saved step and flip saves time. Both forms find better K2000 cuts at every step budget than five published binary-spin algorithms at their papers' settings. Twelve engines at 250 MHz on an AMD Alveo V80 reach a cut of at least 33,000 with 99% probability in 0.05 ms, 5.2 times faster than the fastest published hardware, at 5.4 mJ per solution; with 2-bit couplings, the temperature-scaled form is also faster than uncorrected SCA on 49 of 51 G-set graphs. On an NVIDIA GH200 GPU, the same engine is 2.3 times slower and needs 8.0 times more energy per solution, though its 240 concurrent anneals give 2.3 times the throughput. As a GlobalFoundries 22 nm ASIC at 1.25 GHz, twelve engines would reach the target in about 10 microseconds, 26 times faster than the fastest published hardware. The code is available at https://github.com/skethz/anechoic.

item.title: Strict Dirichlet Pólya Inequality for Simply Connected Planar Domains
item.dc:creator: Quanyu Tang, Zuoqin Wang
item.description:
The main strict Dirichlet Pólya theorem and a strict Neumann analogue were formalized in Lean 4, assisted by Harmonic's Aristotle and OpenAI's Codex.
We establish the strict Dirichlet Pólya inequality on every bounded simply connected planar domain. The proof uses a unitary boundary transport formulation of the Helmholtz equation and relates Dirichlet resonances to unitary eigenphase crossings through the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map. An exact area identity yields the sharp Weyl coefficient, while a Ky Fan estimate leaves a strictly positive remainder in the counting estimate. The general case follows by conformal exhaustion.

item.title: The order types of the supports of $p$-adic algebraic Hahn series
item.dc:creator: Shanwen Wang, Yijun Yuan
item.description:
All main theorems are formalized sorry-free in Lean 4 with mathlib4, built by agentic autoformalization systems on a standalone library, TrustworthyKedlaya.
Let $p$ be a prime number. In 1986, David Lampert asked if one expands a $\mathbf{Q}_p$-algebraic number as a $p$-adic Hahn series, then what is the possible order type of its support? In 2001, Kedlaya made a vague conjecture that the possible ordinals can only be finite ordinals, $ω$ and $ω^ω$, where $ω$ is the first infinite ordinal. In this article, we solve Lampert's problem by confirming Kedlaya's intuition. Moreover, we completely characterize the $\mathbf{Q}_p$-algebraic numbers with order type of support at most $ω$. As an application, we determine the bi-algebraic set of the $p$-adic shadow map.

item.title: Sequential Conformal Calibration under Recursive Selection
item.dc:creator: Yuning Yang, Zexuan Liu, Tianci Wang, Danlin Li
item.description:
Deterministic and algebraic cores of the conformal-calibration theory are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with probabilistic steps entering as named hypotheses.
Conformal prediction provides finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantees that can support decision-making in specific settings. In multistage problems, earlier decisions determine the populations relevant to later calibration. When later scores are refit using earlier calibration results, reusing those cases for ranking need not preserve exchangeability with a surviving test case. We study sequential conformal calibration with a fresh fold at each stage: conditional on earlier folds, the selected fold scores and the surviving test score are exchangeable. This yields finite-sample coverage guarantees for every prefix of the decision sequence. For atomless survivor score distributions, we derive a universal Binomial-thinned Beta chain for the realized coverage process. Its law depends only on fold sizes and target levels, even under predictable refitting, and yields exact coverage slack, abstention probabilities, and calibration-conditional guarantees. We further characterize the tradeoff between freshness and data reuse. For fixed scores, strict-survivor reuse is exactly valid. For adaptive scores refit using past calibration data, reusing survivors can incur worst-case rank loss, while blocked designs provide an intermediate option between full reuse and stagewise fresh folds. As a case study, we apply the framework to serial multi-echelon inventory problem and propose a sequential conditional-quantile formulation. Each stock level is learned as a context-dependent quantile of cumulative demand among scenarios satisfying earlier no-backlog constraints. We connect these targets to common-shift stationarity and derive decision-level implications for the resulting calibrated policies. In a three-echelon simulation, fresh-fold refitting achieves 81.98% final-prefix coverage against an 81.82% target while reducing mean cost by 5.5% relative to the Bonferroni baseline.

item.title: A Catalytic Algorithm for Transposing Unknown Qutrit Unitaries with Tight Query Bounds
item.dc:creator: Yu-Ao Chen
item.description:
Formalizes the paper's exact results (Secs. S1–S5: catalytic transposition circuit, query lower bounds, repeated-use constructions) in Lean 4 with Mathlib, provided as ancillary sources.
We construct exact deterministic circuits for transposing and inverting an unknown qutrit unitary $U\in\mathrm{SU}(3)$ using only forward queries. Three queries prepare a catalyst independently of the input state. Four further queries implement transposition while returning the catalyst unchanged and uncorrelated with the output. Two uses within an antisymmetric encoding implement inversion with eight processing queries and return the same catalyst. Reusing the catalyst implements $m$ transpositions or inversions with $3+4m$ or $3+8m$ total queries, respectively. More generally, we prove that exact transposition and inversion of an unknown $U\in\mathrm{SU}(d)$, $d\ge2$, require at least $d+1$ and $d^2-1$ processing queries, respectively, in fixed causal order. These processing bounds hold for any program state prepared independently of the input state using finitely many forward queries, even if that state is consumed during processing. Both our catalytic qutrit algorithms attain their respective bounds. Moreover, exact qutrit transposition with four processing queries requires at least three preparation queries, and our construction attains this bound.

item.title: On the Five-Point Case of Mordell's Problem
item.dc:creator: Tiancheng Xu, Guowei Dou, Wensheng Yu
item.description:
The five-point Mordell discriminant inequality and both directions of its equality case are fully formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, including verified interval-bound checks.
For five complex points $z_1,\ldots,z_5$ satisfying $\sum_i|z_i|^2=5$, Mordell's discriminant inequality states that $\prod_{i<j}|z_i-z_j|^2\leq5^5$, with equality precisely for a unit regular pentagon, up to rotation and permutation. We organize its proof around a direct comparison of discriminant values. A global maximizer gives a centered stationary configuration, whose coefficient equations reduce the generic case to two quartic branches. On each branch, the absolute value of a cubic polynomial gives the original discriminant objective after accounting for the normalization scale. Exact rational interval bounds exclude both branches from the maximum, and the exceptional coefficient cases leave the regular pentagon. The argument determines the maximizing configuration without reconstructing all stationary shapes. We have completed a full Lean formalization of the five-point inequality and both directions of its equality condition, including all reductions and finite checks used in this proof.

item.title: Codimension-one holomorphic Anosov diffeomorphisms
item.dc:creator: Jiesong Zhang
item.description:
The main theorems and the Ghys results they rely on were formalised in Lean by a Peking University team using the SHEAF formalisation agent.
We prove that every codimension-one holomorphic Anosov diffeomorphism of a compact connected complex manifold is biholomorphically conjugate to a hyperbolic automorphism of a complex torus. This verifies a conjecture of Ghys in the codimension-one case and, in particular, in complex dimension three.

item.title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
item.dc:creator: Anna Mei, Michael R. Douglas
item.description:
Builds an agentic Lean autoformalization pipeline for the NIST DLMF and verifies Lean statements using LLM semantic review, numerical checks, and vacuity checks.
We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://github.com/annamei1/FLMF-Ch7ErrFunc-Release.git.

item.title: MolLean: A Process-Verifiable Language for Chemical Reasoning
item.dc:creator: Jiatong Li, Yatao Bian
item.description:
Implements a Lean kernel that checks molecular state transitions and structural assertions for LLM chemical reasoning, with Lean-proved soundness of valence and connectivity validation.
Chemical chain-of-thought can contain hallucinated structural and property claims. We thereby introduce MolLean, a process-verifiable language that grounds chemical reasoning in an explicit molecular state. A layered Lean-based kernel checks state transitions and assertions over molecular readouts, from primitive graph edits to compound transformations. Meanwhile, a typed witness protocol separates native structural checks from externally supplied measurements. We further introduce MolLean-MCP, a stateful tool interface that exposes these transitions, checks, and readouts during generation: the model receives feedback to decide its next action, and rejected actions leave the state unchanged. MolLean supports one-pass trace execution, whole-trace refinement, and interactive reasoning through MolLean-MCP. We evaluate these three modes with direct chain-of-thought on 8,800 matched examples across 12 tasks spanning molecular generation, editing, optimization, and reactions. With Qwen3.6-27B, whole-trace refinement outperforms direct chain-of-thought on all 12 tasks. MolLean-MCP complements whole-trace refinement with stepwise verification feedback, reaching better performance in reaction tasks. Together, these results highlight an executable foundation for chemical reasoning, in which explicit chemical commitments can be checked and revised rather than remaining solely in free-form explanations.

item.title: Generation by lazy and invertible cellular automata over the Klein four-group
item.dc:creator: Edgar Alcalá-Arroyo, Alonso Castillo-Ramirez, Haobo Ma, Wenlin Zhang
item.description:
The membership criterion and the cardinalities 59,712 and 4,007 are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, kernel-checked without native_decide, in supplementary material.
Let $G=C_2\times C_2$ and $A=\{0,1\}$. We characterize the submonoid of $\text{CA}(G;A)$ generated by lazy and invertible cellular automata. A cellular automaton belongs to this submonoid if and only if, whenever it maps the two free $G$-orbits onto the same free orbit, it maps both constant configurations and some two-point orbit to the same constant. The proof gives a factorization using elementary orbit collapses and three two-cell lazy maps. The criterion yields the cardinality $59\,712$ and identifies the maps missed by a weaker constant-separation invariant. Adjoining one idempotent generates the full monoid, and the generated submonoid is contained in exactly one maximal proper submonoid, of cardinality $65\,024$. The submonoid generated by lazy maps alone has $4\,007$ elements, and for both generating sets the maximum shortest-word length is six. The criterion and the cardinalities $59\,712$ and $4\,007$ are formally verified in Lean.

item.title: Undirected Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
item.dc:creator: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu
item.description:
Formalizes the external-memory sorting theorem (correctness and I/O bounds) and the network-coding counterexample in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with a public repository.
Network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas routing only forwards them. The Li-Li conjecture asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same capacity region in undirected multiple-unicast networks. We give a counterexample to this conjecture and apply it to external-memory integer sorting. Since Aggarwal and Vitter posed the question in 1988, whether integer sorting can beat the external-memory comparison bound has remained a central and extensively studied open problem. We give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $Θ(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $O\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right)$, where $\varepsilon>0$ is an absolute constant. In a range of parameter regimes, this bound is asymptotically smaller than the classical comparison-sorting bound. We also use Lean 4 to verify the sorting algorithm's correctness and complexity bounds, and the strict advantage of coding over routing.

item.title: Verifying deployed bytecode against executable EVM semantics, with exact gas and no added axioms
item.dc:creator: Seulkee Baek
item.description:
Builds Blanc, a Lean 4 stack that verifies deployed EVM bytecode against Jaune, an executable Lean EVM semantics, using kernel-checked certificates and no added axioms.
Much of Ethereum's most consequential code is immutable bytecode: old output of unverified compilers, and protocol logic run as contract code. We show that such bytecode can be verified as it is, without trusting what produced it, without simplifying the machine it runs on, and with no axioms beyond Lean's own. Blanc, a Lean 4 verification stack, reads fixed runtime bytes via kernel-checked certificates and states every theorem against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing that passes all 34,205 blockchain-test cases of Ethereum's fixture release v20.0.2 that involve only forks that have governed mainnet since May 2025. Eight artifacts, deployed from 2017 to 2026, come from seven compiler versions and an assembler. For the EIP-7002 contract, we prove that the end-of-block call to it, whose failure would invalidate the block, succeeds whatever its storage holds, and that each block's withdrawal requests are exactly the oldest pending submissions; mainnet met these theorems' starting premises when Prague began. For a Uniswap V2 pair, we prove that after any valid history whose hashed slots stay apart, from any checkpoint representing its Solidity model's state, the storage represents that model replayed over exactly the committed calls, a balanced liquidity ledger stays balanced, and, under a premise on token answers, geometric-mean reserves per share fall only through the protocol fee. Exact gas makes liveness provable: a tracked WETH9 holder without code can withdraw by a transaction whose gas has a closed form, matching all 3,748 comparable mainnet receipts of its shape in 30,000 blocks. On Curve pool bytes compiled with the lock bug exploited in 2023, Jaune executes such a reentrancy from deployment; for bytes from a fixed compiler, we prove the lock excludes it. AI agents wrote the proofs in fifteen days under one author's direction, atop an existing stack.

item.title: L3M: A Verifiable Harness and Runtime for Self-Extending and Self-Improving Agents
item.dc:creator: Carson Eisenach, Robert Joseph George, Vincent Quenneville-Belair, Kate Gwimm, Dean Foster
item.description:
Implements an agent harness runtime in Lean 4, proves kernel-checked safety theorems about its code, and has agents extend it with sealed Lean programs.
The lasting gains in AI have come from methods that absorb more computation, and language models already scale computation within a call. Useful work, though, happens across calls: over hours or days, through tools and external systems, among many agents and the humans they work for, and increasingly through code the agents write themselves. Whether that work compounds is enabled by the harness around it, and the harness faces a constraint the model does not: of the three participants in such a computation, the human, the model and code, only the human's attention does not scale, so the computation can grow only if the human is not in every loop. L3M is a runtime built on that premise, written in Lean 4 so that one language implements the harness, states its invariants, and is the language agents extend it in. One computation spans humans, agents, models and code, and all of its state lives in Git: a rich state trajectory – rather than a chat conversation – is an object the runtime can resume, rewind, fork, compare and merge. Waiting, communication, delegation and undo are primitives, not patterns the model reasons through each time. When an agent works out a procedure, it can write it once as a sealed Lean program whose type is its permission request, and the harness offers it back as a tool – machinery for the model to use. To take the human out of the loop, L3M uses reversibility to decide where that is safe: a tool's review tier follows from how far its effects can be undone, so agents act freely where the runtime can recover. Because the machinery can change, the properties that make this safe are stated as kernel-checked theorems about the code that runs. On Terminal-Bench, an untuned L3M reaches about two thirds of its (unsafe) shell-equipped pass rate using only safe (not needing human review) tools.

item.title: A short open space curve of unit width
item.dc:creator: Tinko Sebastian Bartels, Dennis Kevin Choy, Ruixiang Wu, Tongxin Li
item.description:
Supplies a Lean 4 formalization (using Mathlib and LeanCert) of the curve's length bounds, local minimality, and interval-arithmetic width certificate, generated with AI assistance.
In this work, we propose a curve to be a minimum of length among rectifiable, continuous curves of unit width in three-dimensional Euclidean space. We show that a previously conjectured minimizer of that problem is not of unit width, give the numerical derivation of a candidate family of unit width curves, prove that it admits a strict local minimum within that candidate family and that this minimum is of unit width and length $3.905124162243593\ldots$. The curve consists of eight straight segments, two cone geodesics, and three circular helices. Its parameters are specified by a uniquely isolated solution of the joining and stationarity equations. To establish unit width in every direction, we combine analytic estimates with interval arithmetic on a finite covering of the remaining directions. We conjecture that the curve is globally minimizing. We supplement this work with the programs used to identify the candidates, replicate the computer-assisted parts of our proof, as well as a formalization of our proof in Lean.

item.title: Positivity and negativity for $h$-bases for $n$
item.dc:creator: Wouter van Doorn, Pietro Monticone, Melvyn B. Nathanson
item.description:
The main comparison results were first discovered and formally verified in Lean by Harmonic's Aristotle agent; the paper gives new human proofs.
A set $A$ of integers is an $h$-basis for $n$ if every integer in $[0,n] = \{0,1,2,\ldots,n\}$ belongs to the sumset $hA$, that is, can be represented as the sum of exactly $h$ not necessarily distinct elements of $A$. The classical postage stamp problem asks for the largest integer $n_h(k)$ such that $[0,n_h(k)] \subseteq hA$ for some set $A$ of nonnegative integers of size $k+1$. We consider the effect of allowing negative elements. Let $n^{\flat}_h(k)$ be the largest integer such that $[0,n^{\flat}_h(k)] \subseteq hA$ for some set $A$ of integers of size $k+1$ containing at least one negative integer. For $k=2$, we have $n^{\flat}_h(2) < n_h(2)$ if $h$ is odd or $h=4$ and $n^{\flat}_h(2) = n_h(2)$ if $h$ is even and $h \neq 4$. Proofs of these comparison results were autonomously discovered and formally verified in Lean by https://aristotle.harmonic.fun/}{Aristotle}, a formal reasoning agent developed by https://www.harmonic.fun/}{Harmonic}. In this paper we give new proofs of these results.

item.title: Ternary polynomial relations and periods of cusp forms
item.dc:creator: Vasily Ilin, Ken Ono
item.description:
The main theorems (1.1, 1.2) and essential argument are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib by AxiomProver, with no admissions and only standard axioms.
Bachmann and van Ittersum conjectured that every polynomial $f\in\mathbb{Q}[x,y,z]$ satisfying $$ f(x,y,z)=f(y,z,x),\qquad f(x,y,z)+f(-y,x-y,z)+f(y-x,-x,z)=0 $$ is a sum of polynomials in two variables. We prove this conjecture over every field of characteristic zero and determine all homogeneous solutions. Moreover, restriction to $z=0$ identifies the degree $n$ solution space with the space of binary period polynomials of degree $n$ normalized to vanish on both coordinate axes. The solution corresponding to such a polynomial $q$ is $$ f(x,y,z)=q(x,y)+q(y,z)+q(z,x). $$ There are no nonzero homogeneous solutions of odd degree. For even degrees $n$, the symmetric and alternating solution spaces are each isomorphic over $\mathbb{C}$ to the space of weight $n+2$ cusp forms on $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$. The proof connects the polynomial relations with the cohomology of arithmetic groups through the rational Tits building for $GL_3$. Cusp forms enter both the description of the solutions and the proof that there are no others. The main theorems and the essential argument are formalized unconditionally in Lean 4 by AxiomProver.

item.title: Definition Grounding in Theory-Level Auto-formalization
item.dc:creator: Leyan Pan, Christian Szegedy, Frederick Rajasekaran, Robi Bhattacharjee, Gregory Constantine, Wenke Lee
item.description:
Introduces ReuseBench, in which LLM agents formalize definitions and layered statements of textbook theories in Lean 4 on top of Mathlib, and evaluates definition reusability.
LLM-based auto-formalization systems can now generate formally verified Lean code at unprecedented rates. However, a formalization advances mathematical research only when further mathematical results can be built on it, especially when its definitions and helper lemmas are general enough to be imported and used idiomatically. We propose definition grounding, where definition formalizations are continuously judged and revised, as a method to ensure formalization quality. We find that agents formalizing definitions from textbook text often produce definitions that later statements cannot use, and only 25%-50% of their definition sets are compatible with all later statements. However, clarifying the informal definitions can improve this rate up to 77.5% averaged over all models. Furthermore, stating a small set of basic properties without proving them can improve model judges' capability to detect definitions with compatibility issues, at only about 11% of the definition formalization cost. These results are verified with ReuseBench, a benchmark we curated for formalizing new mathematical fields and theories.

item.title: Majority and Torus Polynomials: Bounded-Lift Lower Bounds and Explicit Constructions
item.dc:creator: Saint Wesonga
item.description:
Lower bounds and explicit torus polynomial constructions for Majority are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, including Paturi's approximate-degree characterization, with a public repository.
Bhrushundi et al. (2019) introduced torus polynomial approximation as an approach to separating Majority from $ACC^0$. In this model, approximation is measured modulo integers. Krishan and Vishwanathan (2026) developed a duality framework for lower bounds and posed five open problems. We resolve two of these, concerning integer lifts and explicit polynomial approximations. An integer lift records the integer shifts that turn a torus approximation into an ordinary real approximation. We show that a degree-d torus polynomial approximating Majority with error at most 1/8 and lift contained in an interval of width $B$ must satisfy $d(B + 1) = Ω(n)$. This rules out low-degree approximating polynomials with lifts in {-1, 0, 1}, answering their Open Problem 2. We also answer Open Problem 5 by giving, for every Boolean function on $n \geq 1$ variables, an explicit torus polynomial approximation of degree at most $n - 1$. Its error is optimal: zero when the accepting set has even cardinality and $2^{-n-1}$ otherwise. The results presented were discovered and formalized in Lean using GPT-6 Astra.

item.title: Transmission representation of the Josephson free energy beyond the short-junction limit
item.dc:creator: Anton R. Akhmerov
item.description:
Every numbered equation is printed from a theorem or definition checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib, formalized by AI agents and released on Zenodo.
Beenakker's formula, $U(\varphi)-U(0)=Δ\sum_n\bigl(1-\sqrt{1-τ_n\sin^2(\varphi/2)}\bigr)$, expresses the zero-temperature energy-phase relation of a short Josephson junction through its normal-state transmission eigenvalues. We generalize this transmission representation beyond the short-junction limit and express the phase-dependent free energy of a time-reversal-symmetric $s$-wave junction as a Matsubara sum over channels with frequency-dependent transmissions. The representation constrains the small-phase expansion of the free energy. In particular, we prove that the normalized ratio of its quartic and quadratic coefficients satisfies $-1\leα_r\le7/80$ at finite temperature. We also construct a four-site junction with $α_r>0$, which disproves the conjectured upper bound $α_r\le0$. So that these results can be trusted without repeating the derivations, every numbered equation is formally verified in the Lean proof assistant.

item.title: Improved Sidorenko bound for hypergraph Turan densities
item.dc:creator: Shuyan Chen, Xinmin Hou, Xizhi Liu
item.description:
The main Turán density bound, the finite embedding assertion used in its proof, and the existence of the Turán density are formalized in Lean 4.
For every fixed integer $r\ge3$, we prove that the Turán density of every $r$-uniform hypergraph $F$ with $m\ge1$ edges satisfies $π(F)\le1-c_rm^{-(r-1)/r}$, where $c_r>0$ depends only on $r$. This improves Sidorenko's general bound, whose gap from $1$ is of order $m^{-1}$. Complete $r$-uniform hypergraphs show that the exponent $(r-1)/r$ is optimal. The proof combines a potential argument for partial embeddings with the Lovász Local Lemma.

item.title: Certifying non-existence of integer points on curves
item.dc:creator: Bogdan Grechuk, Eugene Go
item.description:
Insolubility proofs for 209 Diophantine equations, including large cubic-reciprocity certificates, are formalized in Lean 4, with Lean code partly generated by ChatGPT.
We present an elementary but powerful method for proving that a two-variable equation has no integer solutions. The method produces quadratic identities which every integer solution must satisfy. Once these identities are established, a standard quadratic reciprocity argument finishes the proof. We illustrate the power of the method by resolving $25$ out of $30$ two-variable equations of size up to $34$ for which the problem of integer solubility remained open. We also resolve the remaining $5$ equations by deeper methods, and further determine the integer solubility of all two-variable equations of size up to $35$ and of length up to $12$, with two exceptions. Before this work, there were $211$ equations in this category that resisted the previously known methods, and we proved that $209$ of them have no integer solutions, with all proofs formalized in Lean. In addition, we show that our method can be used to solve certain two-variable equations whose integer solution set is non-empty.

item.title: An improved lower bound for the minimum-autocorrelation constant
item.dc:creator: Shenai Chen, EnHao Gu
item.description:
A Lean 4.19.0/Mathlib development formalizes the Bernstein certificate, overlap integrals, admissibility, mass formula and ordinary-function witness bounds for the autocorrelation lower bound.
We construct nonnegative bounded compactly supported functions on the real line that give the lower bound $\mathcal{A}\ge 0.4103779774321214877852987\ldots$ for the minimum-autocorrelation constant. This improves the explicitly certified bound $2378625/5958277=0.39921356\ldots$ reported by Russell. The construction combines a point mass with a monotone degree-ten polynomial density; a one-sided atom-removal argument then produces ordinary functions. Its numerical content reduces to exact rational polynomial identities and 20 Bernstein subinterval certificates. The finite certificate, actual overlap integrals, admissibility, mass formula, and ordinary-function witness bounds have been formalized in Lean 4.19.0; the pinned proof sources and recorded audit are supplied. The passage to the supremum constant is given separately as a mathematical argument. As applications, the same construction yields an upper bound below $1.5610183$ for the large-multiplicity generalized-difference-basis coefficient and a feasible squared mass below $2.436778$ for a continuous sparse-ruler relaxation. An appendix quantifies the loss under independent sampling followed by completion. No improved bound for the complete sparse ruler constant, or global optimality of the construction, is asserted.

item.title: Global asymptotic stability of homogeneous polynomial vector fields is undecidable
item.dc:creator: Ivan O. Shevchenko, Jun Liu, Xinzhi Liu
item.description:
The main undecidability and cubic-reduction results are formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, with an accompanying repository mapping statements to Lean and an axiom audit.
We study the decision problem of global asymptotic stability (GAS) of the origin for homogeneous polynomial vector fields with rational coefficients. In the first part of the paper we give, for every fixed dimension $n$ and odd degree $2k+1$, a computable map which sends a homogeneous vector field of degree $2k+1$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ to a homogeneous cubic vector field on $\mathbb{R}^m$, $m=\binom{n+k-1}{k}$, and preserves both GAS and Lyapunov stability. The map passes to new variables $y_α=x^α$ (one for each monomial $x^α$ of degree $k$), in which the vector field becomes cubic, and adds a cubic penalty term transverse to the set of points of the form $(x^α)_{|α|=k}$; the main point is that this controls every initial state of the new system. As a consequence, the GAS problems for all degrees, for each fixed odd degree $d\ge3$, and for degree three are pairwise many-one equivalent. In the second part we prove that there are a fixed dimension $N_*$ and a fixed odd degree $d_*$ such that the set of homogeneous vector fields on $\mathbb{R}^{N_*}$ of degree $d_*$ whose origin is GAS is many-one complete. The reduction encodes an undecidable family of polynomial equations in integer unknowns into the constant term of a product of Jacobi theta series, realizes these series as outputs of a polynomial differential system with rational coefficients, and turns the existence of an integer solution into the sign of a maximal invariant average, which homogeneous GAS detects. Combining the two parts shows that GAS of rational homogeneous vector fields on $\mathbb{R}^N$ of degree $d$ is many-one complete for every odd $d\ge3$ and every sufficiently large $N$; in particular it is undecidable for cubic vector fields in a fixed dimension. Building on recent work, some analogous results are proven for Lyapunov stability of homogeneous vector fields.

item.title: Tiling 3D by Translates of a Single Polycube is Undecidable
item.dc:creator: Erik D. Demaine, Stefan Langerman
item.description:
The full undecidability proof for single-polycube translational tiling is formalized in Lean 4 on Mathlib, building on the lean-wang Wang-tiling formalization.
We prove co-RE-completeness, and thus undecidability, of the following problem: given a single (connected) polycube, decide whether it tiles 3D Euclidean space by translations. We reduce from Wang tiling using the decorated two-prime Sudoku construction of Greenfeld and Tao and a cyclic encoding adapted from OpenAI's 3D aperiodic tile, and apply a reduction of Kim to make the prototile connected (via faces). Dimension three is optimal: translational monotiling is known to be decidable in $\mathbb{Z}^2$ and for a single (possibly disconnected) polyomino in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

item.title: Curating Always-Loaded Context for LLM Agents: A Capacitated Assortment Model with Censored Feedback
item.dc:creator: Zexuan Liu, Yuning Yang, Tiancheng Zhao
item.description:
Nearly all numbered theorems on context-file curation, except those relying on one smoothness assumption, have complete formal proofs in Lean 4, supplied as supplementary material.
At the start of every session, LLM agents load a fixed context file, such as $\texttt{AGENTS.md}$. Each loaded token in the file is charged again in every later round of the session, and these files can degrade performance as they grow in size. However, in practice, human or automated curators usually grow these files by appending. We formulate context curation as a capacitated assortment problem. Instructions consume tokens under a finite attention capacity; adding an instruction never raises the compliance of the others, while retained instructions incur a per-session setup cost. We prove an upper bound on the optimal file size, regardless of the number of available candidate instructions, and that appending every instruction with positive standalone value can be arbitrarily worse in net value than selecting an optimal subset. A token budget also limits the loss when the token price is underestimated. We then examine what can be learned from past sessions and how this information can guide decisions to add or remove instructions. Feedback is inherently censored: the benefits and harms of loaded instructions are observable, whereas missing instructions generate feedback only when their absence causes harm. In this setting, we show that deleting instructions ignored by agents can inevitably remove helpful ones. We characterize how much evidence should be collected before adding an instruction. Besides, we bound regret when human reviewers can inspect only a limited number of edits per period. Empirical experiments further show that irrelevant rules drawn from real context files reduce language-model compliance.

item.title: Tweaking the constant in the Linear Hadwiger Theorem
item.dc:creator: David R. Wood
item.description:
The main theorem bounding chromatic number by 19,885,160 times Hadwiger number is formally verified in Lean 4 with Mathlib, extending Norin–Steiner's Lean formalisation; files are ancillary.
Norin and Steiner recently proved the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture. That is, there is an absolute constant $C$ such that every graph $G$ satisfies $χ(G)\leqslant C\,\text{had}(G)$, where $χ(G)$ is the chromatic number and $\text{had}(G)$ is the Hadwiger number of $G$. Their proof gives a non-optimised constant $C$ of order $10^{100}$. This paper uses extensive AI-based optimisation to show that every graph $G$ satisfies $χ(G) \leqslant 19{,}885{,}160\,\text{had}(G)$.

item.title: Towards Verifying Neural Networks Against Multi-Parameter Bit-Flip Perturbations
item.dc:creator: Hai Duong, Thanh Le, Ho Nguyen, ThanhVu Nguyen
item.description:
Soundness propositions of the bit-flip verifier (top-m bound, LP relaxation exactness, branch-and-bound correctness, propagation counting) are mechanized in Lean 4 with Mathlib.
Hardware faults can flip bits in the stored weights of a quantized neural network, potentially compromising its predictions. While such faults typically affect multiple parameters simultaneously, existing verifiers are limited to single-parameter perturbations due to the combinatorial explosion of possible flip locations in large networks. We present mBFV (m-BitFlip Verifier), an efficient verification framework that proves robustness against simultaneous bit flips across multiple parameters without explicitly enumerating these combinations. mBFV achieves this via a novel multi-parameter bound propagation technique that directly aggregates the m worst-case contributions. To further tighten these bounds, mBFV employs a branch-and-bound mechanism over perturbation locations, partitioning the potential flips to smaller groups of neurons. Evaluated on 625 instances, mBFV successfully verifies 293, significantly outperforming a prior single-parameter verifier (38 verified instances) and an exact mixed-integer linear programming baseline (0 verified instances). Notably, while these baselines are restricted to single-parameter flips on small networks (up to 13k parameters), mBFV scales to verify networks with up to 1.15M parameters against up to four simultaneous parameter flips.

item.title: The Aharoni–Korman conjecture is false
item.dc:creator: Lawrence Hollom
item.description:
The key Proposition 2.2 of the counterexample was formally verified in Lean by Bhavik Mehta, with the code available in Mathlib4.
A poset $P$ is said to satisfy the finite antichain condition, or FAC, if it has no infinite antichain. It was conjectured by Aharoni and Korman in 1992 that any FAC poset $P$ possesses a chain $C$ and a partition into antichains such that $C$ meets every antichain of the partition. In this work we provide a counterexample to this conjecture, demonstrating that it is false. We also discuss variations of the conjecture which may yet be true.

item.title: Selecting the 7th Smallest of 16 Elements Takes Exactly 28 Comparisons
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Cremer
item.description:
Lean 4 kernel-checks the decision-graph certificates for all seven new selection upper bounds; a separate Mathlib-based development formalizes the partial-order leaf lower bound.
Let $V_i(n)$ denote the minimum worst-case number of comparisons needed to find the $i$-th smallest of $n$ distinct elements. We construct algorithms showing $V_7(16)\le28$ and $V_8(16)\le29$, improving the previously reported upper bounds of 30 and 31. Together with known lower bounds, these results establish $V_7(16)=28$ and leave $V_8(16)\in\{28,29\}$. For 17 elements, we establish $V_5(17)=27$ and improve the upper bounds for ranks 6 through 9 to 29, 30, 31, and 31, respectively. Every new upper bound has an explicit decision-graph certificate verified by a static checker developed independently of the search. We also derive a lower bound for selection from a partially ordered state by combining the Fussenegger-Gabow weight with its order-reversed counterpart. All new upper bounds and this lower bound are formally verified in Lean 4. For $V_8(16)$, we show that a lower bound based solely on the total number of decision-tree leaves cannot establish $V_8(16)\ge29$. The algorithms were found using fixed-budget search, information-guided comparison ordering, and proof-number search. Proof-number search was decisive in finding the 28-comparison algorithm; in our experiments, refuting a comparison budget remained substantially more expensive than finding an algorithm within it.

item.title: A Central Limit Theorem for High-Temperature SYK Model
item.dc:creator: Yoshinori Kamijima, Shuta Nakajima, Ryoichiro Noda, Kôhei Sasaya
item.description:
Main CLT proofs for the SYK free energy were formalized in Lean 4 using AI-generated code reviewed by humans, conditional on one annealed free-energy proposition.
The Sachdev–Ye–Kitaev (SYK) model is a quantum many-body model of Majorana fermions with all-to-all random interactions. It has attracted wide interest in condensed matter and high-energy physics as a solvable model of non-Fermi liquids and holography. Fix an even integer $q\geq4$, and let $Z_N(β)$ be the partition function of the Gaussian $q$-body SYK model. We prove that for all sufficiently small inverse temperatures $β> 0$, there exists $ρ=ρ(β)>0$ such that \[ N^{q/2 -1}(\log Z_N(β)-\mathbb{E}[\log Z_N(β)]) \Longrightarrow \mathcal{N}(0,ρ^2). \] In addition to the mathematical results, we discuss how the proofs were developed and refined through interaction between human researchers and AI, and we describe the subsequent formalization of the main arguments in Lean 4. This work thus serves as a case study of a research workflow that integrates human insight, AI-assisted exploration, iterative proof refinement, and formal verification.

item.title: Prescribed and simultaneous failures of log-concavity in trees with perfect matchings
item.dc:creator: Heshun Fan
item.description:
The parameterized counterexample theorems, quantitative ratio bounds, and the 90-vertex example are formally proved in Lean 4 with Mathlib's SimpleGraph independent sets.
We construct trees with perfect matchings and independence sequences that fail log-concavity near the independence number $α$. For every integer $k\geq1$, one family fails at $α-k$ and has a witness of order $O(k^2\log(k+2))$. For every integer $t\geq2$, a single tree has simultaneous failures at $α-1,α-3,\ldots,α-(2t-1)$, with a witness of order $O(t^3)$. All these trees satisfy $α=N/2$, where $N$ is the number of vertices, and contradict Conjecture 4.2 of Ramos and Sun. A sufficient condition uses a fixed tree and the numbers of attached leaves. For fixed $k$ or $t$, explicit bounds give geometric decay of $a_j^2/(a_{j-1}a_{j+1})$ at these indices as the trees grow; $a_j$ counts independent $j$-sets. The proofs count independent sets by empty matching pairs. The Lean proof assistant checks formal proofs of the parameterized results and their quantitative bounds; exact 90- and 180-vertex examples illustrate the constructions.

item.title: A dataset of formalised theorem statements from the Annals of Mathematics
item.dc:creator: Thomas Browning, Katerina Hristova, David Ledvinka, Justus Springer, Hang Lu Su, Jack McKoen, Kevin Buzzard
item.description:
Hand-written Lean 4 statements of 50 Annals of Mathematics main theorems, built on Mathlib, released as a LeanEval proving benchmark.
Recent progress in autoformalisation of mathematics using AI has been impressive. Measuring this progress requires datasets of formal statements that are both hard and trustworthy. We present AnnalsChallenge: 50 formalised theorem statements written by hand in Lean 4 using Mathlib. Each is the main result of a paper published in the Annals of Mathematics since 2020. Every formalisation was manually reviewed and then audited by AI. We release them without formalised proofs.

item.title: Goodman-type lower bounds for odd cycles I: The dense regime
item.dc:creator: Seonghyuk Im, Taeyoung Kim, Hongseok Yang
item.description:
The odd-cycle Goodman-type lower bound and strengthened commonality inequality are formalised in Lean 4, with the formalisation produced largely by Claude models.
Goodman proved a lower bound on triangle counts which, in graphon language, states that every graphon of edge density $p$ has triangle density at least $2p^2-p$. Bennett, Dudek, Lidický, and Pikhurko established the corresponding bound for $C_5$, determining its minimum density at every Turán density $p=1-1/k$ with an integer $k\ge3$. We extend this bound to every odd cycle in the dense regime: for every odd integer $m\ge3$ and every graphon $W$ with edge density $p\ge2/3$, $t(C_m, W) \ge p^m-p(1-p)^{m-1}.$ For $2/3\le p<1$, equality holds precisely for balanced complete $k$-partite graphons with an integer $k\ge3$, up to graphon equivalence, and we establish qualitative stability at these densities. In the same density range, we also strengthen Kim and Lee's density-sensitive commonality inequality for odd cycles by adding the nonnegative term $t(P_{m-1},1-W)-(1-p)^{m-1}$ to the lower bound, where $P_{m-1}$ is the path with $m-1$ edges. To prove the main results, we develop a spectral excursion expansion and use Dirichlet averaging to reduce the resulting polynomial inequalities in arbitrarily many spectral variables to a one-variable problem. We prove the one-variable inequality through a uniform inequality comparing odd and even moments of shifted Gamma random variables. We also formalise the odd-cycle lower-bound theorem in Lean 4.

item.title: QEDIA: Quantum Program Verification in Lean
item.dc:creator: Yuanjie, Ren, Zhicheng Zhang, Junyi Liu, Jinzheng Li, Yidi Qi, Mingsheng Ying
item.description:
Formalizes the quantum Hoare logic QHL+ in Lean 4 on Mathlib, proves it sound, and verifies quantum programs using an LLM-based prover agent.
Practical quantum programs interleave quantum and classical computation: classical data shape the quantum operations that are performed, and measurement outcomes shape the classical computation that follows. Formal verification of such programs in a proof assistant requires mechanizing a program logic that handles this interplay consistently at every level, from the mathematics of quantum mechanics, through program syntax and semantics, to specifications and proof rules. Such mechanizations, along with the program proofs built on them, typically require substantial manual effort. We present QEDIA, a framework for verifying quantum programs with classical variables in Lean 4. At its foundation is an open library that formalizes the quantum Hoare logic QHL+ across all these levels and proves the logic sound for both partial and total correctness. We construct the library and the program proofs, under human supervision, using an LLM-based prover agent, whose general-purpose core we extend for quantum program verification. We illustrate QEDIA with verified programs including the quantum Fourier transform, phase estimation, repeat-until-success circuits, and Hamiltonian simulation.

item.title: LeanPRM: Lean-Grounded Process Supervision for Natural Language Proof Verification
item.dc:creator: Rodney Lafuente-Mercado, Salman Rahman, Jingyan Shen, James Shiffer, Saadia Gabriel, Pavel Izmailov
item.description:
Uses Lean 4 to check paired formal tactic steps, turning compile outcomes into step-level correctness labels for training natural-language proof verifiers.
AI systems now write long and difficult mathematical proofs, and checking their step-by-step validity is becoming a bottleneck. A learned verifier could check proofs cheaply, but training one requires a correctness label on every step, and such labels are hard to obtain for open-ended proofs. Existing methods take them from human annotators, which is costly, or derive them from final answers, which proofs do not have, and formalizing each proof in Lean requires expert effort. We introduce LeanPRM, a framework that uses the Lean proof assistant to create step-level labels for natural-language proofs. A model writes a natural-language proof together with a paired formal proof, without feedback from Lean. Lean then labels every step, and a second model discards failures caused only by the formal syntax, so that the negative labels mark errors in the mathematics. LeanPRM contains 10,634 proofs with 152K labeled steps and no human annotation. A Qwen3-4B verifier trained on LeanPRM raises exact step-label accuracy on a held-out set of 200 proofs (LeanPRM-Bench) from 48.2 to 74.7, as opposed to 60.3 when the same base model is trained on PRM800K. It also selects better proofs in best-of-N selection on IMO-level problems, and outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on three of four external verification benchmarks. Training on LeanPRM improves verifiers at every size from 0.6B to 8B parameters on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify and IMO-GradingBench. Given the labels need no human annotation, LeanPRM can grow with the supply of formal statements, offering a path to step-level feedback on AI-generated proofs that are hard for humans to check.

item.title: VeriPIE: Checkable Query Plans and Evidence-Guided Selection for Text-to-SQL
item.dc:creator: Piyush Jha, Cruise Song, Zhengyu Li, Yatharth Sejpal
item.description:
Implements the QuerySketch plan language's parser, elaborator, and typed relational core in Lean to check and lower LLM-generated query plans to SQL.
Financial Artificial Intelligence (AI) governance and model risk management (MRM) emphasize independent validation, transparency, and effective challenge of AI-generated computations. Text-to-SQL translates natural-language questions into Structured Query Language (SQL), but queries that agree on one database can still express different computations. We present VeriPIE, a neurosymbolic framework combining language-model generation with symbolic checks. It ensembles direct SQL generation with QuerySketch, a structured plan language checked by a backend implemented in Lean, a theorem prover and programming language. Plan diagnostics guide repair before SQL generation, while execution agreement and bounded searches for distinguishing databases inform candidate selection. These checks expose malformed plans and hidden disagreement without proving agreement with the user's intent. In single-run experiments on the complete Spider development set, VeriPIE achieves 72.05% test-suite accuracy (745/1,034), compared with DeepEye's 65.67% (679/1,034). Its two-query shortlist covers 78.43% (811 questions), compared with 74.66% for DIN-SQL (772) and 69.05% for DeepEye (714). On BIRD, VeriPIE reaches 68.90% execution accuracy and 73.73% two-query coverage. The central benefit is reviewable evidence about the generated computation: explicit plan checks, repair diagnostics, and concrete disagreements that support safer financial analysis.

item.title: Thin matrix products up to D <= N^0.172 and lossless reductions for 3SUM, Exact Triangle and APSP, with 3SUM over abelian groups and a dichotomy for coordinatewise problems
item.dc:creator: Ruhollah Majdoddin
item.description:
Most of the paper's mathematics, including algorithm correctness, counts, exponents and the dichotomy theorem, is formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib in a public repository.
Alman and Vassilevska Williams (arXiv:2610.06783) gave the first polynomial improvements over the textbook algorithms for 3SUM and APSP: deterministic algorithms with exponents 1.9992 for 3SUM, 2.9983 for Exact Triangle and 2.99942 for APSP. Their algorithm has two steps: a matrix theorem, computing N^2/sqrt(D) prescribed entries of the product of an N x D and a D x N integer matrix in time N^2/D^gamma, gamma > 0, when D <= N^eps, for every eps < 0.1204; and reductions from the three problems to the lopsided sparse triangle problem. We improve both. With Schönhage's five-term partial-product tensor, the matrix theorem holds for every eps < 0.172. The preprint's reductions keep a quarter of the matrix theorem's saving for 3SUM and a half for Exact Triangle and APSP; ours keep all of it, by calling the counting version of the triangle problem adaptively and building composite moduli one prime at a time. Together this gives deterministic 3SUM in n^{1.9945+o(1)}, and Exact Triangle, (min,+)-product and APSP in n^{2.9945+o(1)}. We also improve on the preprint's proof sketch for 3XOR and solve it deterministically in O(n^{1.99451}). Which other problems on three lists does the method make truly subquadratic? It solves 3SUM over F_p^d for every fixed prime p with 3XOR's exponents, and over every finite abelian group of exponent p^2, such as Z_4^d, in O(n^{1.99726}). For coordinatewise problems with a fixed relation P on every coordinate triple, a certified exhaustive computation shows that every Boolean P, and every functional P over three letters, either is the solution set of an equation over Z, F_2 or F_3, and the problem is then truly subquadratic, or has a gadget for Orthogonal Vectors, and the problem is then hard under the Orthogonal Vectors hypothesis. Over four letters, just four functional relations, up to symmetry, satisfy neither condition.

item.title: claimcheck: Measuring and Improving Specification Faithfulness
item.dc:creator: Martin Amster, One An, Holly Baker, Fernanda Graciolli, Simon Henniger, Nada Amin
item.description:
Builds a spec-faithfulness benchmark including 1,296 Lean 4 PutnamBench rows, using Lean tactics to prove meaning-preserving control rewrites equivalent.
Formal verification proves that a program satisfies its specification, but says nothing about whether the specification captures what the author meant. As LLMs increasingly write both code and specifications, a gap between the author's natural-language requirement and the specification becomes a live risk. A machine-checked proof of a property narrower than the one requested is worthless but passes every check. Closing this gap is solving the spec formalization problem: given a natural-language requirement, produce a formal artifact whose meaning matches it. To measure the gap, we curate an end-to-end benchmark for spec formalization spanning four formal languages: Dafny contracts and Lean 4, Isabelle and Rocq theorem statements. Each of its 3,234 rows pairs a natural-language requirement with a formal artifact and a label established by execution, by proof, or by the benchmark it is drawn from. A third of the rows are meaning-preserving rewrites of the artifact that keep the faithful label, so a judge cannot score by detecting that a row was edited. We introduce claimcheck, a tool that detects incorrect formalizations: the formal artifact is translated back into plain English by a model that never sees the requirement, and a separate model, the judge, decides whether the informalization and the requirement express the same guarantee. On all four languages it gains 8.2 to 9.8 points of macro recall over a single call shown the requirement and the artifact, and 4.2 to 6.0 over that call handed the same list of meaning-preserving rewrites. Showing the judge the artifact as well costs 1.4 to 4.5 points. Across four judges that also see the artifact, the gain shrinks as the judge gets stronger, to within a point of the informed single call for the strongest.

item.title: Higher derivatives of the Gram function
item.dc:creator: Marius Dundulis, Ramūnas Garunkštis, Antanas Laurinčikas, Raivydas Šimėnas
item.description:
Formalizes asymptotics of higher derivatives of S(t) and Gram functions and uniform distribution results in Lean 4, with code written largely by LLMs.
We study the nonlinear phenomenon of the asymptotics of higher-order derivatives of the Gram function $t_u$. We also prove the uniform distribution and continuous uniform distribution modulo one of $t^n_u$ for $n = 1, 2, \dots$. We use AI to formalize our proofs in Lean.

item.title: Do Theorem Provers Need Theorem-Proving Agents? mini-Lean-agent: A Coding-Agent Baseline for Lean
item.dc:creator: Tomas Ortega, Simon Park, Ayush Khaitan, Liam Fowl, Alex Kontorovich, Sanjeev Arora
item.description:
Builds a bash-only coding agent that searches Mathlib and invokes Lean 4 to prove Putnam 2025 problems, with a separate trusted Lean checker validating proofs.
General-purpose coding agents use standard shell and file interactions, yet formal theorem-proving agents often rely on specialized, ad-hoc tooling. This makes it difficult to determine which components of theorem-proving agents provide benchmark gains: an improved base model, a specialized harness, a specific tool, or a combination of any of them. We introduce mini-Lean-agent, a deliberately minimal agent for Lean tasks whose only model-visible tool is bash. The model must use bash to inspect and edit the repository, search local libraries, invoke Lean, and manage its own intermediate work, while a separate trusted evaluator verifies the final artifact. We compare mini-Lean-agent against AxProverBase and Numina-Lean-Agent on the Putnam 2025 benchmark. Experiments with Gemini 3.8 Flash as the base model show that mini-Lean-agent solves 7/12 problems at \$2 per problem limit, compared with AxProverBase's 4/12. With Astra as the base model, mini-Lean-agent solves 12/12 problems at an average cost of \$1.28 per problem. This suggests that a generic coding agent with a minimal harness can already achieve strong performance on Lean benchmarks. Our results motivate using mini-Lean-agent as a standard baseline when evaluating theorem-proving infrastructure.

item.title: Quantum Cryptography and Autoformalization in Lean
item.dc:creator: Maor Ben Shahar, Jonathan Morag, Dirk Englund, Kfir Sulimany
item.description:
End-to-end composable finite-key security of entanglement-based BB84 formalized in Lean 4 with Mathlib, developed via LLM-agent autoformalization; library released open source.
Quantum key distribution provides secure communication by relying on physics principles and mathematical reasoning. Security proofs across the field can contain gaps, often between individually valid theorems integrated under mismatched assumptions. We produce an end-to-end security theorem formalized in the Lean proof assistant, eliminating hidden hypotheses by building only on Lean's standard axioms. Our proof covers composable security of the entanglement-based qubit BB84 protocol against coherent attacks by the postselection technique, accounting for finite block size, and is written in a language that enforces local operations and classical communication to help ensure a faithful representation of the protocol. The proof itself was enabled by LLM-based autoformalization, and with the proof complete, we used the same pipeline as a discovery machine, reducing the finite-size penalty on the key rate. Our work sets a reproducible standard for security arguments in quantum cryptography and shows how formal proof engines can accelerate discovery across quantum information science.

item.title: Finite-order exponential mixing does not imply the central limit theorem
item.dc:creator: Bernat Bassols Cornudella, Matheus M Castro
item.description:
The main Theorems A, B and C, plus the external results they rely on, are formalised in Lean 4 with Mathlib, using only the standard axioms.
We show that finite-order exponential mixing does not imply the central limit theorem for smooth diffeomorphisms. For every integer $R\geq2$, we construct a $\mathcal{C}^{\infty}$ diffeomorphism $T:M\to M$ of a compact smooth manifold $M$ and a $T$-invariant probability measure $μ$ such that $(T,μ)$ is exponentially mixing of order $R$ for $\mathcal{C}^1(M)$ observables, but not of order $2R+2$. For some centred observable $f_0\in\mathcal{C}^{\infty}(M)$, no subsequence of the normalised sums $\frac{1}{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}f_0\circ T^i$ converges in distribution to a Gaussian law. In particular, exponential decay of two-point correlations implies neither exponential mixing of all orders nor the central limit theorem. We realise $(T,μ)$ in two ways. In the first, $T$ is a fixed linear Anosov diffeomorphism of $\mathbb T^2$ and $μ$ is singular with respect to Lebesgue measure. In the second, $M$ can be any compact smooth surface without boundary and $μ$ is a physical measure whose statistical basin contains a nonempty open set. The main theorems have been formalised in Lean 4.

item.title: Masked Attention Pooling Is Invariant to Padding and Permutation: A Formal Proof in Lean
item.dc:creator: Yusuf Khaled Sadek, Enes Yilmaz
item.description:
Proves padding and permutation invariance of masked attention pooling in Lean 4 with mathlib, and links the proofs to traced JAX code via jax-lean certificates.
Attention-based multiple instance learning (MIL) pools a variable-size bag of instance embeddings into one vector. In batched training, bags are padded to a common length, and the pooled output is expected not to depend on how much padding was added or on the order in which instances are stored. This expectation holds only if padded rows are removed from both the numerator and the softmax normalizer. Common implementation idioms meet it only under side conditions. Zeroing padded features alone does not work. Masking logits with $-\infty$ fails on empty bags and on nonfinite padding. Masking with a large negative constant is exact only after floating-point underflow. We define masked attention pooling with a guarded normalizer and prove in Lean 4 with mathlib that it is invariant under any bijective reindexing of rows and under appending any finite number of masked rows with arbitrary real features and logits. We also prove that values at masked positions are irrelevant and that an all-masked bag maps to zero. The theorems hold for arbitrary finite index types and feature dimensions. Using the jax-lean certificate pipeline, we connect these theorems to the Jaxpr traced from the JAX kernel itself. Lean checks translation certificates for two concrete shapes, identifies the generated functions with the generic specification, and transfers both invariances to the imported Jaxpr's real-arithmetic semantics. All audited theorems depend only on Lean's three standard axioms. The results concern ideal real arithmetic. Floating-point execution, XLA, and the JAX tracer and importer remain outside the proof.

item.title: CLASSO: a practical primal path-following algorithm for the constrained LASSO
item.dc:creator: Michael Hobson, Luke Butcher, Lindley Lentati
item.description:
The well-posedness, piecewise-affine path finiteness and termination theorems, plus counterexamples, are formalised in Lean 4 against Mathlib with no admitted proofs.
We present CLASSO, a path-following method for the LASSO subject to general linear equality and inequality constraints. The local direction is obtained from a quadratic programme on an augmented active set, which determines both the coefficients that leave zero and the weakly active inequalities that remain binding. For a positive-definite Hessian and a nonempty feasible set, this programme has a unique primal minimiser, even when the binding constraint rows are dependent, and gives the local derivative of the solution path. The construction recovers the LASSO-modified LARS direction without constraints, and over the full cone gives the segment leaving the origin. We prove that the primal path is piecewise affine with finitely many kinks, without a constraint qualification or unique multipliers. A finite path does not imply a finite traversal: re-certifying at each kink can fail to terminate. CLASSO instead follows the minimum-norm certificate along a lexicographic rate; we prove that this rule reaches $λ=0$ in exact arithmetic within an explicit bound and traverses the whole path. These results are machine-checked in Lean 4, and the floating-point implementation agrees with an exact rational one on all $210$ small test problems. We assess the implementation on a $39$-case synthetic suite and six constrained versions of the diabetes benchmark. On the $31$ nontrivial synthetic cases with $n\ge p$, sampled relative objective differences from numerical reference solves are below $10^{-9}$ in magnitude; unnormalised endpoint differences reach $1.5\times10^{-7}$ in magnitude. For $n<p$, matched differences range from $-3.6\times10^{-7}$ to $2\times10^{-9}$ across five ridge strengths. Across the synthetic and diabetes benchmarks, checks of all $580$ recorded segments found no missed interior event and all checked KKT residuals within the stated tolerances.

item.title: The Bloch constant is strictly smaller than the Ahlfors–Grunsky value
item.dc:creator: Teng Zhang
item.description:
